item.title: Nginx, from HTTPS to a WebSocket proxy
item.description: On top of the minimal setup that serves frontend files and forwards /api, the HTTPS, caching, compression, WebSocket, SSE and timeout settings you add on a server.
item.content:encoded:
The previous post built a minimal setup that serves the frontend files and forwards /api to the backend. This post covers what you add to that setup when it goes onto a server, grouped by purpose, so each line in the configuration file has a reason next to it.

HTTPS

Line What it does
listen 443 ssl Accepts HTTPS on port 443
ssl_certificate The certificate. A public file shown to the browser
ssl_certificate_key The certificate’s private key. A file that must not leave the server
ssl_protocols The TLS versions to allow. Leaves out the old 1.0 and 1.1 and opens only 1.2 and 1.3

ssl_certificate takes not just the server certificate but a file with the intermediate certificates from the certificate authority appended (the fullchain). With the server certificate alone the site opens in a browser, but other servers or apps calling the address can get certificate errors. Browsers fetch a missing intermediate certificate on their own; most other clients don’t.

If Nginx runs in a container, mount the certificate folder as a volume and open port 443. Mount the private key read-only (:ro).

A certificate you make yourself for an internal dev server (a self-signed certificate) still encrypts the connection, but browsers show a warning because it was not issued by a trusted authority.

Don’t turn on HSTS in that case. HSTS is a Strict-Transport-Security response header that tells the browser “open this address over https only from now on”. A browser that has received it removes the button for proceeding past a certificate warning. A self-signed certificate always triggers the warning, so with HSTS on, the address can’t be opened at all.

Requests that arrive over http

Some people type http:// into the address bar. There are two cases.

When ports 80 and 443 are open separately, the server on 80 only redirects to the https address.

When only one port is open, with HTTPS, an http:// request to that port gets a 400 error page saying “The plain HTTP request was sent to HTTPS port”. Inside Nginx this case has its own code, 497, and you can redirect that code to the https address.

$http_host is the host and port exactly as the browser sent them, so an address with a port such as :8443 keeps it.

Lines that differ from the http setup

Moving an http setup to https changes only a few places.

http https
listen listen 8080; listen 8080 ssl;
Certificate none ssl_certificate, ssl_certificate_key, ssl_protocols
Requests arriving over http not applicable 80 → 443 return 301, or error_page 497 on the same port
X-Forwarded-Proto the backend receives http the backend receives https
Running the container port plus dist and config file volumes add the certificate folder volume
Cache, compression, location unchanged unchanged

X-Forwarded-Proto is already among the proxy headers in the previous post, so the line stays as it is and only its value becomes https. The backend talks to Nginx over http, so without this header it can’t tell that the browser came in over https. Redirect addresses the backend builds then go out as http://, and cookies meant only for https (Secure) are not handled. The backend also has to be set to read the header. In Spring Boot this is server.forward-headers-strategy.

Caching

A browser can keep a file it has downloaded and skip downloading it next time. The server says how long to keep it with the Cache-Control header. The frontend files fall into two groups that are handled differently.

File Setting Reason
JS and CSS under /assets/ keep for a year, don’t ask again The file name changes on every build. Same name means same content
index.html keep, but check with the server before each use The name never changes. It holds the names of the newly deployed JS and CSS

As the previous post showed, a build produces names like index-3f9a1c2e.js, and the name changes when the code changes. So files in assets/ can be kept for a long time without an old file ever being used. A new version arrives under a new name.

The problem is index.html. If an old copy is kept, it points to the old JS name, and you get a deploy that doesn’t change what the user sees. So index.html is checked with the server every time.

no-cache doesn’t mean “don’t store”; it means “check before using”. If nothing changed, the server answers with a short 304 and the browser uses its stored copy. Not storing at all is no-store, which downloads the whole file every time.

There is one more reason to give /assets/ its own block. Without it, a request for a JS file that doesn’t exist also goes through the try_files in location / and gets index.html back. The browser tries to read HTML as JS and reports an error that is hard to make sense of. try_files $uri =404 returns 404 for missing files instead.

Once a location has even one add_header, the add_header lines in the enclosing server no longer apply to that location. If you put security headers in server, keep this in mind.

Compression

Text files such as JS and CSS shrink a lot when sent gzipped. The browser adds Accept-Encoding: gzip to the request to say it accepts compressed responses, and Nginx compresses what it sends back.

Line What it does
gzip on Turns compression on
gzip_types File types to compress. text/html is always included without being listed
gzip_min_length Responses smaller than this are not compressed. For small files the cost of compressing outweighs the saving
gzip_vary Adds Vary: Accept-Encoding to the response

PNG and JPG are already compressed formats, so they stay out of gzip_types. Compressing them again saves almost nothing.

gzip_vary matters when a caching proxy or CDN sits in front of Nginx. It says that the same address has a compressed and an uncompressed version, so a client that can’t take compressed responses doesn’t get the compressed one.

If there is another proxy in front of Nginx, such as a load balancer, Nginx by default doesn’t compress those requests. Add gzip_proxied any; in that case.

Check compression with the response headers.

gzip_comp_level sets the compression level from 1 to 9. The default is 1. A higher level makes files a little smaller and uses more CPU.

WebSocket

WebSocket opens a connection once and lets the server and browser keep sending messages over it. It is used for live notifications and monitoring screens. The /api setup from the previous post doesn’t connect it; it needs a few more lines.

A WebSocket starts as an ordinary HTTP request and asks to “switch this connection to WebSocket” with an Upgrade: websocket header. But by default Nginx talks to the backend over HTTP/1.0 and doesn’t pass the Upgrade and Connection headers on. The backend never receives the switch request, and the connection fails.

Line What it does
proxy_http_version 1.1 Talks to the backend over HTTP/1.1. Switching connections only works in 1.1
Upgrade, Connection headers Pass the browser’s switch request on to the backend
proxy_read_timeout Keeps the connection open this long even when nothing is sent

proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 seconds. A WebSocket can be quiet for a while, and after 60 seconds with no message Nginx closes the connection. Either set the value longer, or have the client and server exchange a short signal (a heartbeat) at intervals. A longer value means dead connections are cleaned up later, but quiet connections stay open.

Local development is the same. When the Vite proxy setting forwards a WebSocket path, it needs ws: true. As the previous post said, path rules have to be written in both places.

SSE

SSE (Server-Sent Events) is the server sending a continuous stream of events to the browser, in one direction only. Unlike WebSocket it is one ordinary HTTP response that just doesn’t end, so it needs no connection-switch headers. It needs different lines instead.

Line What it does
proxy_buffering off Passes the backend response straight to the browser instead of collecting it
proxy_http_version 1.1, Connection "" Keeps the connection to the backend open instead of closing it after one response
proxy_read_timeout Keeps the connection open even when there are no events for a while

By default Nginx collects the backend response in a buffer before sending it. That is efficient for ordinary responses, but with SSE the events pile up in the buffer and reach the browser much later, all at once. So proxy_buffering off turns it off. The backend can also turn buffering off for a single response by adding an X-Accel-Buffering: no header to it.

For the same reason, text/event-stream stays out of gzip_types. While Nginx collects data to compress, the events arrive late.

Timeouts

How long Nginx waits on a request it forwarded to the backend is split into three settings.

Directive What it waits for Default
proxy_connect_timeout Opening a connection to the backend 60s
proxy_send_timeout Sending the request to the backend, from one write to the next 60s
proxy_read_timeout Reading the backend response, from one read to the next 60s

None of the three is a total time. Each is the gap between two operations. If the response keeps arriving, even in small pieces, the connection isn’t closed after 60 seconds.

The 504 Gateway Timeout from the previous post is a request that hit proxy_read_timeout. If something legitimately takes long, such as an API that builds and returns a large file, you can raise the value for that location only. Raising it everywhere means that when the backend hangs, requests are held that much longer.

If there are file uploads, also look at client_max_body_size. It is the maximum request body size and defaults to 1MB, so uploading a larger file gets 413 Request Entity Too Large from Nginx before the request reaches the backend.

nginx.conf and conf.d

The official image has its configuration in two layers.

File What it holds
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf Settings written once for all of Nginx. Process count, log format and location, and the line that loads the folder below
/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf Settings for one site. The server block with its listen, certificates, root and locations

nginx.conf

This is the first file Nginx reads when it starts. Trimmed down, the one in the official image looks like this.

The include at the end of the http block pulls in the files from conf.d/ at that spot. So the server block in default.conf is the same as one written inside this http block.

File names

The two files differ in how fixed their names are.

File Name
nginx.conf Fixed. Nginx is built to read /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
default.conf Not fixed. The include is conf.d/*.conf, so any file ending in .conf is read, whatever its name

default.conf is just the name of the file the official image ships. It holds a server block that shows the Nginx welcome page on port 80.

So if you mount your configuration under a different name (such as app.conf), the original default.conf is read as well. If the two server blocks use the same port, requests can end up in the wrong one. Mounting your configuration over default.conf avoids this.

Repositories often keep per-environment names such as nginx.dev.conf and default.prod.conf, and map them to the fixed paths when mounting them into the container.

Nginx only sees the paths inside the container, so the file names outside can be anything.

Which file to write in

Everything in this post and the previous one can go in default.conf. gzip and client_max_body_size can be written inside the server block too. When running a single app, edit only default.conf, and mount nginx.conf when you want to change the log format or location.

There is one thing to watch when the same directive appears in both files. If an inner block has the same directive, the outer value is ignored entirely. It isn’t partly overridden.

The path is the same, so it looks like the same setting, but the main format doesn’t apply in the server block. A value you leave out isn’t inherited from outside; it goes back to the default. add_header from Caching follows the same rule. That’s why log settings go in nginx.conf only.

Whichever file you changed, apply it the same way as in the previous post: check with nginx -t, then nginx -s reload.

Settings at a glance

Goal Setting
Accept HTTPS listen 443 ssl; + ssl_certificate, ssl_certificate_key
Send http to https return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
Send http on the same port to https error_page 497 =301 https://$http_host$request_uri;
Always check index.html add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
Keep assets for a long time add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
Compression gzip on; + gzip_types …
WebSocket proxy_http_version 1.1; + Upgrade, Connection headers
SSE proxy_buffering off; + a long proxy_read_timeout
Wait longer for the backend proxy_read_timeout 300s;
Allow larger uploads client_max_body_size 20m;

item.title: Nginx, from static files to an API proxy
item.description: The two jobs that appear when one Java app serving pages and an API is split into a frontend and a backend, and how to set them up with Nginx.
item.content:encoded:
When one Java app that served both pages and an API is split into a frontend and a backend, two jobs appear that did not exist before: who serves the built frontend files, and who forwards the browser’s API requests to the backend. This post covers how those two jobs work in each environment, and how to do them on a server with Nginx.

Single application and split structure

A service built as one Spring Boot app has that one app receive every request. A request to / gets HTML built by the app; a request to /api gets JSON. One container, one address.

Build the frontend separately with React or Vue and things change. Running npm run build on the frontend produces a dist/ folder with index.html plus JS and CSS files. These are just files; they cannot receive requests on their own. Something has to serve them to the browser. The backend now handles only the API.

Single application Split structure
Pages The Java app builds and returns HTML Built files. A separate program has to serve them
API The Java app The backend
What runs One thing Two things

That raises two questions. Who serves the frontend files? And how does a /api request from the page reach the backend?

One address, split by path

Put the pages and the API at different addresses and the browser gets in the way. A browser treats two addresses as the same origin only when the scheme, host and port all match. With the pages on :8080 and the API on :8100 the origins differ, and unless the backend sends back CORS headers, the browser will not let the page read the response. Passing login cookies back and forth gets complicated too.

So the usual setup is to put one program in front, collect everything under one address, and split by path.

From the browser’s side there is only one address, so there is no origin problem. The program in front looks at the path, forwards /api to the backend, and answers everything else with the frontend files. A program like this is called a reverse proxy.

Proxies and reverse proxies

A proxy is a program in the middle that receives a request on someone’s behalf, passes it on, and returns the response it gets back. The English word literally means acting on someone’s behalf.

Proxies split into two kinds by which side they sit on.

Proxy (forward proxy) Reverse proxy
Which side The requesting side. In front of the browser The receiving side. In front of the servers
Who knows it exists The browser is configured to use it The browser does not know. It thinks that address is the server
What it hides The requester. Servers see the proxy as the one asking The servers behind it. The browser never learns the backend’s address
Example The proxy a company network routes outbound traffic through Nginx forwarding /api to the backend

Plain “proxy” usually means the first kind, a forward proxy. What Nginx does in this post is act as a reverse proxy. The browser only knows app.example.com and has no idea the frontend files and the backend live separately behind it.

The proxy in setting names means the same thing. Nginx’s proxy_pass and the proxy in Vite’s config are both reverse-proxy settings that forward requests to the backend behind them.

Who does it in each environment

That reverse proxy is a different program in each environment.

Serving the frontend files Forwarding /api
Local development The Vite dev server (npm run dev) server.proxy in vite.config.ts
Dev server · production Nginx Nginx’s proxy_pass

You can develop locally without Nginx because the Vite dev server does the same job. The dev server started by npm run dev serves the pages and forwards the paths listed under proxy in its config to the backend.

The backend runs separately, started from the IDE or Gradle. The browser only sees localhost:5173, and the dev server forwards anything starting with /api to localhost:8100.

The dev server is for development only. It includes features that reflect code changes on screen immediately, and it is not meant to be deployed. On a server, Nginx serves the dist/ built by npm run build.

Because the two environments do the same job with different config files, the path rules have to be written in both places. Add /auth to the forwarding rules in vite.config.ts, forget it in the Nginx config, and it works locally but returns 404 on the server.

Building dist

The files Nginx serves are built from the frontend project. This assumes Vite.

npm ci instead of npm install installs the same versions every time. Use it when building on a server or in CI.

A finished build leaves a folder like this.

One index.html and a few bundled JS and CSS files. The string after each file name is derived from the contents, so rebuilding after a code change changes the names.

Build modes and environment variables

If dev and production settings differ, build with a mode. Building with --mode dev reads the .env.dev file.

Values starting with VITE_ are written into the JS files at build time. They are not read while running on the server, so changing one means rebuilding.

That is why it is easier to write the API address as a path only, like /api, rather than putting something like https://api.example.com in an environment variable. With the pages and the API at the same address, a path alone reaches the API, and the same build output works on the dev server and in production.

Putting it on the server

Put dist/ in the folder Nginx’s root points to. There are three ways.

Mount as a volume Copy into the image Build inside the image
Build npm run build outside the container npm run build outside the container Inside the Dockerfile
Image The official nginx image as is nginx + dist/ nginx + dist/
Deploying a new version Replace the host’s dist/ folder Build outside, then rebuild the image Rebuild the image
Build environment Can differ per PC or CI Can differ per PC or CI Fixed in the Dockerfile

Mounting as a volume means adding -v /opt/web/dist:/usr/share/nginx/html to docker run. The examples in “Connecting containers” below use this.

Copying into the image just puts a dist/ built elsewhere into the image.

The Dockerfile is short and the image is small. The catch is that the build machine needs Node, and different Node versions on different machines can produce different results.

Building inside the image splits the build and the runtime.

The first stage builds with Node; the second carries over only dist/ and the config. Neither Node nor the source code ends up in the final image. Splitting one Dockerfile into stages like this is called a multi-stage build.

Skip the stages and do both building and serving in a single node image, and Node, node_modules and the source code all stay in the final image, pushing it to hundreds of megabytes. None of that is used on the server.

Nginx configuration

A minimal config that serves the frontend files and forwards /api. With the official image it goes in /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf.

server and location

A server block is the set of settings for one port. The location blocks inside it decide what happens per path.

When a request path matches several locations, the longest match wins. /api/users matches both / and /api/, but the longer /api/ handles it. So / can stand for “everything else” and only the paths that need special handling get their own block.

Static files — root and try_files

root is the folder to look for files in. A request for /logo.png returns /usr/share/nginx/html/logo.png.

Without try_files, refreshing the page returns 404. Page addresses in a React or Vue app are not files. An address like /history/12 is something the JS in the browser created while changing the screen; there is no such file in dist/. Navigating inside the app works fine, but refresh at that address and the browser asks the server for a /history/12 file, which Nginx does not have.

try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html tries each in order.

Order Looks for Example: /logo.png Example: /history/12
1 $uri — a file with that name Found → returned Not found
2 $uri/ — a folder with that name Not found
3 /index.html Returned → the JS draws the /history/12 screen

API proxy — proxy_pass

proxy_pass forwards the request to the backend. upstream gives the backend address a name. You can also write the address directly, as in proxy_pass http://192.168.0.20:8100;.

Once requests go through Nginx, the client the backend sees is Nginx, not the browser. These four headers carry the original request’s details to the backend.

Header Carries
Host The domain the browser requested
X-Real-IP The browser’s IP
X-Forwarded-For The list of IPs along the way. The first is the browser
X-Forwarded-Proto Whether the browser came in over http or https

The backend reads these when it logs client IPs or builds redirect URLs. Leave them out and every request appears to come from Nginx’s IP.

Whether proxy_pass ends in / changes the path the backend receives. Follow a browser request for /api/users.

  • Without the /, the request path is passed along untouched. /api/users goes as is
  • With the /, the /api/ that matched the location is removed and replaced with the / written in proxy_pass. /api/ in /api/users becomes /, giving /users

Which one to use depends on the backend’s controller paths.

If the backend returns 404 while the Nginx log shows the request arriving, look here first.

Connecting containers

With Nginx and the backend in separate containers, the question is what to write as the backend address in the Nginx config.

localhost does not work. Inside a container, localhost is that container itself. There is no backend inside the Nginx container, so the connection is refused.

There are two ways.

Using the host IP

No Docker network needs to be created. Publish the backend’s port on the host with -p, and write the server’s IP and that port in the Nginx config.

Nginx goes out of its container to port 8100 on the server, and that port leads into the backend container. If the backend is on a different server, only the IP changes.

The IP to write is the server’s IP. A container IP like 172.17.0.x shown by docker inspect can change when the container is recreated, so it does not go in the config.

Using a Docker network

On the same Docker network, Docker resolves container names to addresses. Create a network and start both containers on it.

Here the backend does not need to publish its port with -p. The browser only goes through Nginx, and Nginx reaches the backend inside the network.

The difference

Host IP Docker network
Setup None docker network create
Address in the config 192.168.0.20:8100 backend-app:8100
Publishing the backend port Required Not needed
Backend on another server Works Does not. Same server, same network only
If the server’s IP changes The config has to change No effect

How to run the containers themselves is in the Docker post.

Checking and applying the configuration

After editing the config, check the syntax first, then have Nginx reload it if the check passes.

Reload while nginx -t is failing and Nginx keeps running on the old config. When a change seems not to take effect, look at nginx -t first.

The official image sends its access and error logs to the container’s output, so docker logs shows them directly.

These are the response codes you will see most.

Code Meaning Where to look first
404 (only on refresh) No file for that page address try_files
404 (from the backend) The backend received a different path The / at the end of proxy_pass
502 Bad Gateway Nginx could not connect to the backend The backend address and port, whether the backend container is running
504 Gateway Timeout The backend did not answer in time How long the backend takes. The default wait is 60 seconds

Command reference

What you want Command / setting
Folder for the frontend files root /usr/share/nginx/html;
Avoid 404 on refresh try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
Send /api to the backend location /api/ { proxy_pass http://backend; }
Name the backend address upstream backend { server host:port; }
Check syntax nginx -t
Reload the config nginx -s reload
Watch the logs docker logs -f web
Create a shared network docker network create app-net

item.title: Using Redis from Spring
item.description: What each redis-cli command maps to in Java, and why values written from Java can be unreadable in redis-cli.
item.content:encoded:
What Redis is and how to look at it in redis-cli is in the earlier post. This one covers how to use Redis from Spring.

Dependency and connection settings

If the Redis has a password, set password. Do not write it into the config file as is; take it from an environment variable. Leave it out and the first command fails with NOAUTH; get it wrong and the connection fails with WRONGPASS.

These are the settings you will use most.

Setting Meaning Default
host Redis address localhost
port Port 6379
password Password none
database Database number. Used when several apps share one Redis by number (0–15) 0
timeout How long to wait for a single command’s reply 60 seconds
connect-timeout How long to wait while first establishing a connection 10 seconds

Leave timeout out and it is 60 seconds. If Redis stalls, requests wait that long along with it. A short timeout fails fast when something goes wrong, but a command that legitimately takes a while can also fail partway. Decide by how long the commands your app sends actually take. A bare number like 3000 is read as milliseconds.

In Spring Boot 2.x the setting was spring.redis.host. In 3.x it became spring.data.redis.host. If the old name is still there, the value is not applied and the app tries localhost:6379 and fails.

With the starter on the classpath, a StringRedisTemplate is created for you. Inject it.

opsForXxx and Redis data types

RedisTemplate and opsForXxx() are names Spring Data Redis chose, not Redis. What Redis defines is the commands — SET, HSET and so on — and the job of actually sending them belongs to the driver underneath, Lettuce (the Spring Boot default). Spring Data Redis sits on top, handles connections and serialization, and groups the commands by data type into methods.

Method Returns Redis data type
opsForValue() ValueOperations String
opsForHash() HashOperations Hash
opsForList() ListOperations List
opsForSet() SetOperations Set
opsForZSet() ZSetOperations Sorted Set

The first row is the confusing one. What Redis calls the String type, Spring calls Value. The rest share the same names.

Commands that act on a key regardless of its data type, like DEL, EXPIRE and TYPE, sit directly on the template: redis.delete(), redis.expire().

You can chain onto opsForXxx() every time. With opsForHash(), though, chaining leaves the field and value types as Object. The types are taken from the variable that receives the result, and a chained call has no such variable.

Assign it to a variable once and the types are fixed.

The others — opsForValue(), opsForList() and so on — use the template’s types as they are, so chaining them needs no cast.

Serialization

Inject a plain RedisTemplate instead of StringRedisTemplate and the keys and values become unreadable in redis-cli.

This is what redis-cli shows.

Even the key name is unrecognizable.

That is because RedisTemplate serializes with JDK serialization by default. It turns Java objects into bytes, so outside Java the data can neither be read nor found under the same key.

StringRedisTemplate stores keys and values as plain strings.

When you need to store a whole object, serialize it to JSON and store the string. Then redis-cli can read it too.

Stored as a string, the value can be read directly in redis-cli or a GUI tool. You need that when checking whether something like a session went in wrong. A value stored with JDK serialization can only be read through Java code.

String

increment raises a stored number and returns the value after raising it. Counting visits per day looks like this.

A missing key starts from 0. A second argument raises it by that much. The return value is a Long, and Redis stores it as a string.

Calling it on a key that holds something other than a number is an error — for example increment on session:a1b2c3, which holds "user=1000".

Hash

HashOperations<H, HK, HV> takes three type arguments: the key type, the field type and the value type, in that order.

List

For a list of recent items, trim right after pushing.

Set

There are two ways to check membership, and the gap grows with the number of members.

isMember takes about the same time whether there are ten members or a million. A Set goes straight to the value internally instead of walking from the start. With members, a million members means a million values over the network before the search even starts.

Sorted Set

reverseRange returns only the values; reverseRangeWithScores includes the scores. A leaderboard has to show scores too, so the second one is the usual pick.

Expiry

getExpire returns -1 for a key with no expiry and -2 for a key that does not exist.

Setting the expiry together with the value is safer. Call set and then expire separately, and an exception or a dead process in between leaves a key with no expiry.

What happens to the expiry when you change a value depends on the data type. Overwriting a String with set clears the expiry it had. To keep an expiry, pass it again when you overwrite.

Changing a Hash field with put does not touch the key’s expiry. The expiry time you set stays as it was.

Key lookup

redis.keys() looks like an ordinary method, but it sends the KEYS command as is. KEYS walks every key in the database, not just the ones matching the pattern, and Redis handles no other command while it does. The concepts post said KEYS * is not used in production; adding a pattern like session:* does not narrow what gets walked. The reason is in Commands are lined up and handled one at a time in the concepts post.

Application code rarely needs to find keys. It knows the ID, so it builds the key and reads it directly. When you need a list, do not search for keys — store the list as well when you store the data. If you need the list of active sessions, it looks like this.

Reading the list means reading sessions:active alone. It does not matter how many other keys the same Redis holds.

One catch: Set members have no expiry. When the session key expires after 30 minutes, its ID is still in sessions:active. Remove IDs whose session key is gone when you read the list, or clean them up periodically.

When you occasionally have to walk the keys — checking keys in production, or cleaning up old keys in bulk — use scan(). It fetches in small pieces, so Redis keeps serving other commands.

Close the Cursor when you are done so its connection is released.

Concurrent updates

To raise a number, use increment instead of reading with get and writing back with set. With more than one server, the latter drifts.

Here is visit counting without increment. Do not write it this way.

On a single server there is no problem. With two servers running this at the same time, it goes like this.

Step Server A Server B Value in Redis
1 get → 10 10
2 get → 10 10
3 set 11 11
4 set 11 11

Two increments, and the value is 11. Both read 10 before either wrote.

increment does the read, the add and the write inside Redis as a single command. Redis handles commands one at a time, so nothing can slip in between the two servers’ increment calls, and the result is 12.

Storing an object as one JSON string, then get, change a field, set, has the same problem. One server overwrites the field another just changed with the old value. For an object whose fields change separately, store it as a Hash and write only that field with opsForHash().put(). The concepts post shows this as a diagram in JSON string, or a data type.

A number inside JSON cannot use increment. Take settings stored as one JSON blob, with a version raised by one on every save.

To Redis this value is one string, not a number, so increment cannot raise just the version field. If two people save the same settings at nearly the same time, the table above plays out. Both read version 5 and both write 6. On top of that, the JSON saved last overwrites everything saved first. One person’s changes are gone, and since the version went up only once, nothing shows it was saved twice.

To prevent it, send the version the screen read along with the save request, and compare it with the current version before saving. If they differ, someone saved in between, so reject the save. This is called optimistic locking.

A small gap still remains between the comparison and the set. If two requests pass the comparison at once, one still overwrites the other. Closing that gap means doing the comparison and the save inside Redis in one go: watch the key with WATCH and cancel the save if it changed in between, or run the comparison and the save as a Lua script that behaves like a single command. Where simultaneous saves are rare, such as an admin screen, the comparison above is usually enough.

redis-cli commands and their methods

What you want redis-cli Java
Store a value SET k v opsForValue().set(k, v)
With an expiry SET k v EX 1800 opsForValue().set(k, v, Duration.ofMinutes(30))
Read a value GET k opsForValue().get(k)
Increment a number INCR k opsForValue().increment(k)
Set an object field HSET k f v opsForHash().put(k, f, v)
Read a whole object HGETALL k opsForHash().entries(k)
Append to a list RPUSH k v opsForList().rightPush(k, v)
Slice a list LRANGE k 0 9 opsForList().range(k, 0, 9)
Cap a list’s length LTRIM k 0 9 opsForList().trim(k, 0, 9)
Add to a set SADD k v opsForSet().add(k, v)
Is it in there SISMEMBER k v opsForSet().isMember(k, v)
Add with a score ZADD k 120 v opsForZSet().add(k, v, 120)
Top 10 ZREVRANGE k 0 9 opsForZSet().reverseRange(k, 0, 9)
Set an expiry EXPIRE k 1800 expire(k, Duration.ofMinutes(30))
Time remaining TTL k getExpire(k, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
Delete DEL k delete(k)
Check the data type TYPE k type(k)
Find keys SCAN 0 MATCH k* scan(ScanOptions)

item.title: Connecting to a Redis container and checking its state
item.description: Connecting to a running Redis container, checking its state and looking up keys, and connecting a GUI tool to it.
item.content:encoded:
What Redis is and how its data types work is in the concepts post. This one is about connecting to a Redis that is already running in a container and checking its state.

Connecting with redis-cli

If you started it with Docker, redis-cli is already inside the container. There is nothing to install.

Get the name exactly right. If you run containers with a version in the name, it is myapp-redis_1.0.0, not myapp-redis, and a guess gets you No such container. The rightmost column of docker ps is the actual name.

You can also connect in one step, without the shell in between.

The difference: the first way lets you look at config files or run other commands inside the container too; the second is one line when Redis is all you need.

A slim image may not have bash. Use sh instead.

Once connected, the prompt changes to this.

The front is the address and port you are connected to; commands go after the >. exit leaves.

If a password is set, type AUTH your-password first after connecting. Without it every command comes back with NOAUTH Authentication required.

If the port is published to the host and the host has its own redis-cli, you can skip the container and connect directly with redis-cli -h 192.168.0.10 -p 6379.

Checking memory

How much memory is in use right now, and whether keys are being evicted because the limit was hit.

Field Meaning
used_memory_human How much is in use now
maxmemory_human The limit. 0B means there is none
maxmemory_policy What happens when the limit is reached
evicted_keys How many keys were dropped because of the limit

If evicted_keys is not 0, keys are already being thrown away. If you are storing sessions, that many logouts have happened.

Key lookup and monitoring

You can also ask one-off questions without opening a session. For a Redis inside a container, put docker exec myapp-redis in front.

To find keys, use --scan instead of KEYS. It fetches in pieces, so nothing else is blocked.

This finds the keys taking up the most memory.

To watch commands as they go by, use MONITOR. It prints every command, so in production turn it on only briefly.

GUI tools

redis-cli covers a lot, but once there are many keys, scanning a list by eye is faster.

I use Another Redis Desktop Manager. It is open source and free, with Windows, macOS and Linux builds.

Three things made me pick it. Copying a key is one click, values holding JSON show up indented, and you can edit or delete a value in place.

The second one makes the biggest difference. Store an object as a JSON string and redis-cli gives it back as one long line.

Past ten fields or so it is hard to read. In the terminal you have to pipe it through jq.

A GUI expands it for you. If you check values often, that adds up.

You can change values with redis-cli too, but changing one field of a long JSON means typing the whole thing again. A GUI edits and saves in place. It is handy for making test data by hand or fixing a value that went in wrong.

That same feature is dangerous against a production Redis. As the concepts post puts it, a call in progress or a session has Redis as its original at that moment. Delete it by mistake and there is nowhere to restore it from. Some tools delete without asking for confirmation, so it is safer to make production and development connections look clearly different in the list. Putting [prod] in the connection name is enough.

It also folds keys on the colon. With thousands of keys like call:20260922:1000, they group into call → 20260922, so you can open them up to see what kinds there are and how many.

Other tools

Tool What it is
RedisInsight The official tool from the makers of Redis. Free. Analyzes which keys use the most memory and shows the slow command log
DataGrip, IntelliJ Ultimate If you already use JetBrains tools, it sits in the same window
VS Code extensions Browse keys and edit values inside the editor
TablePlus Paid. Relational databases and Redis in one tool
Medis macOS

If you dig into production state a lot, it is worth having RedisInsight installed alongside. Its screen for finding memory-heavy keys is easier to read than --bigkeys, and it gives you something to go on when setting a memory policy.

Search around and the name Redis Desktop Manager comes up a lot. It has since been renamed RESP.app and become paid. It is a different tool from the Another Redis Desktop Manager described here. Pricing changes, so check before you download.

Ports and SSH tunnels

A GUI connects from outside the container, so the port has to be published to the host.

If nothing comes back, it was started for use inside the container only. You have two ways in: go through the server with the tool’s SSH tunnel feature, or docker exec in and use redis-cli.

0.0.0.0 means it is open on every network interface of the host. Anyone who can reach that host can try to connect, so check whether a password is set while you are at it.

An empty value means there is no password. To open it on one interface only, put an address in front: -p 127.0.0.1:6379:6379 instead of -p 6379:6379.

With an SSH tunnel there are two sets of fields to fill in.

What goes in
Host, Port 127.0.0.1, 6379 — the Redis address as the server sees it
SSH Host, Port The server IP, 22
SSH Username Your login on the server
SSH Key, Password Authentication for the server

Writing 127.0.0.1 for the Redis address is the confusing part. It is not your PC — it is the address as seen from the server you tunneled into.

Once connected, think before pressing the button that loads the key list. If that button uses KEYS, all of Redis stops for as long as it runs when there are many keys. Try it against a development Redis first, and use MONITOR from earlier to see which command it sends.

Command reference

What you want Command
Connect from inside the container docker exec -it myapp-redis redis-cli
Check published ports docker port myapp-redis
Memory state redis-cli INFO memory
Evicted key count evicted_keys in redis-cli INFO stats
Number of keys redis-cli DBSIZE
Find keys redis-cli --scan --pattern "session:*"
Find big keys redis-cli --bigkeys
Watch commands redis-cli MONITOR

Using it from Spring is covered in Using Redis from Spring.

item.title: Redis, from the idea to data types and commands
item.description: Almost everything about Redis follows from one fact — the data sits in memory. The five data types and the redis-cli commands that go with them.
item.content:encoded:
What Redis is

A store you put a value into under a key and read back by that key. It keeps that data in memory, not on disk.

The name is REmote DIctionary Server. Think of the Map you use inside a program, lifted out of the process so several servers can share it. Point three servers at the same Redis and all three share the same session.

Nearly every property follows from “it is in memory”.

Because it is in memory What follows
No round trip to disk Responses drop below a millisecond
Memory is the ceiling How much you can hold is tied to the machine’s RAM
It goes when the process goes Keeping anything means configuring a separate write to disk

How it differs from a relational database

Only the places where the habits you already have do not carry over.

Relational DB Redis
Where data lives On disk. Memory is a buffer pool In memory. Disk is for persistence
Data model Tables, columns, types, constraints Key-value. No schema
How you read SQL, with conditions Direct access by key
Joins Yes No
Transactions Commit and rollback, isolation levels Atomic execution, but no rollback
Capacity ceiling Disk size Memory size

A buffer pool is the area where a relational database holds pages it read from disk. The original is on disk; memory is a temporary spot for what gets used often.

Persistence is writing what is in memory out to disk. Memory goes when the process goes, so a copy is kept in a file to bring it back on restart.

Redis is the mirror image. The original is in memory, and what sits on disk is the copy.

If you do not know the key, you cannot find it

This is the largest difference. In a relational database you can store data first and invent the question later.

Redis has nothing like this. To look people up by age, you have to build the list of keys for that condition ahead of time.

So Redis is a store where you decide what you will read and how, then write it in that shape. A relational database runs the other way around, which is why you can put a new condition on data you stored long ago.

There is a KEYS * that walks everything. It is not used in production. The reason is right below.

Commands are lined up and handled one at a time

Redis runs command execution on a single thread. It finishes one and starts the next, in arrival order. (Network I/O is split across threads, but the commands themselves run one at a time.)

That cuts both ways.

  • The good side — no lock contention and no context switching, so each command is very fast. Two commands never touch the same key at once, which makes counters and locks simple to build
  • The side to watch — one slow command blocks everything for its duration. Type KEYS * against millions of keys and every other request waits it out

When you do need to walk the keyspace, use SCAN. It comes back in pieces, so nothing is blocked.

A relational database handles connections in parallel, so one heavy query does not stop the rest. In exchange you have locks and isolation levels to think about.

Where it gets used

Use What goes in Data type
Sessions Login state String, Hash
In-flight state A call in progress, an order being processed Hash
Cache Results of a relational query String
Counters View counts, call volume String + INCR
Leaderboards Top N by score Sorted Set
Distributed locks Making sure something runs once String + SET NX

It is the same Redis, but the reason for choosing it differs by use. Any one of the six below is reason enough, and usually several apply at once.

If you need this For example
A disk round trip is too slow Cache, in-flight state
Several servers have to see the same thing Sessions, distributed locks
It has to survive a redeploy or restart Sessions, in-flight state
It has to disappear on its own after a while Sessions, cache
Concurrent changes must not drift apart Counters, distributed locks
A sorted order has to stay maintained Leaderboards

On that last line: pull a ranking out of a relational database and you sort on every read. A Sorted Set settles the position on write, so the top ten — or one user’s rank — comes back immediately.

The middle three have nothing to do with speed. A Map inside the app process satisfies the first line and none of the rest. A relational database is the opposite: it satisfies everything but the first.

These, on the other hand, are no reason to reach for Redis.

  • Anything you search by condition — without the key you cannot find it
  • Anything you keep for a long time — memory costs more than disk
  • Anything that needs transactions — there is no rollback

It comes down to where the original lives

Example If Redis dies
The original is in the relational DB Cache, leaderboards Read it again and refill
Redis is the original Sessions, in-flight state You lose whatever was in flight

Take a call in progress. For as long as the call lasts, that state exists only in Redis. It reaches the relational database as history after the call ends.

If you are holding things Redis is the original for, persistence and the memory policy have to be decided too. With a pure cache you can skip both.

JSON string, or a data type

There are two ways to put an object into Redis.

As one JSON string,

or as a Hash.

Reading the whole thing, there is barely a difference. What separates them is changing part of it.

Say the call state goes from TALKING to ENDED. The JSON side takes three steps.

The Hash side takes one.

Two things differ here.

How much moves. The JSON side carries the whole object twice to change one field. Thirty fields means thirty received and thirty sent.

Concurrent changes. This is the one that matters.

On the JSON side, server B overwrote everything based on the old value it had read. It never touched state, and yet A’s ENDED is gone.

HSET changes only the field you name. There is no read step, so there is no old value to overwrite with.

So you choose like this.

How to store it
You always read and write the whole thing A JSON string is simpler
You change fields separately Hash
Several servers change the same object Hash

Lists work the same way. A JSON array in a String means a full round trip for every addition; a List makes it one RPUSH.

Connecting with redis-cli

The commands below are entered at the redis-cli prompt. If you are running it as a container, connect like this.

Once connected the prompt becomes 127.0.0.1:6379>. exit leaves. Commands for checking its state and connecting a GUI are in Connecting to a Redis container and checking its state.

The five

Data type What it is Where it fits
String One value under one key Sessions, cache, counters
Hash Fields and values. One object Reading and changing an object field by field
List An ordered list. Push and pop at either end Recent items, a simple queue
Set A collection with no duplicates. No order Deduplication, intersections
Sorted Set A collection ordered by score Leaderboards, time-ordered lists

String

INCR is not a read, add and write back — Redis does it in one go. That is why several servers can raise the same counter without the value drifting.

Hash

The Java equivalents, such as HashOperations, are in part 3.

List

LPUSH to add and LTRIM 0 9 to cut gives you a list that holds the last ten. Trimming on every write is the convention.

RPUSH on one side and LPOP on the other makes a queue. If you need retries or failure handling, reach for a dedicated tool like RabbitMQ — a List queue loses the message if the worker dies while processing it.

Set

SISMEMBER takes the same time no matter how many members there are. That is not what happens when you fetch the whole list and search it in the app.

Sorted Set

Each value goes in with a score, and the collection stays ordered by it.

Put a timestamp in the score and you have a time-ordered list. ZRANGEBYSCORE slices it by period.

Setting an expiry

Give a key a lifetime and Redis deletes it for you once the time passes. That lifetime is called the TTL, for Time To Live.

TTL answers one of three ways.
A positive number Seconds remaining
-1 No expiry. It stays forever
-2 No such key. Already gone, or never there

A relational database has nothing like this. You keep an expiry column and clear it with a batch job, or compare timestamps on every read. That is why “it has to disappear on its own after a while” counts as a reason to reach for Redis in Where it gets used above.

Setting it as you write the value is safer. SET followed by a separate EXPIRE leaves a key with no expiry if the process dies in between.

Keys piling up with a TTL of -1 is a common reason memory keeps filling.

Spring integration

Connecting from Spring is covered separately, along with what each of these commands maps to in StringRedisTemplate.

Command reference

What you want Command
Store a value SET k v
With an expiry SET k v EX 1800
Read a value GET k
Increment a number INCR k
Set an object field HSET k f v
Read a whole object HGETALL k
Append to a list RPUSH k v
Slice a list LRANGE k 0 9
Cap a list’s length LTRIM k 0 9
Add to a set SADD k v
Is it in there SISMEMBER k v
Add with a score ZADD k 120 v
Top 10 ZREVRANGE k 0 9
Set an expiry EXPIRE k 1800
Time remaining TTL k
Delete DEL k
Check the data type TYPE k

item.title: Docker, from the idea to a working Dockerfile
item.description: Putting a single Java jar into a container, in order — writing the Dockerfile, building and running it, getting inside to look around, and carrying it to a server with no registry.
item.content:encoded:
What a container is, how to write a Dockerfile, and how to build and run one. The examples are Java. Picture a single executable .jar from Spring Boot going into a container.

What Docker is

A tool that bundles everything an app needs to run, so the app behaves the same on any server. No more gaps from a different Java version or one missing library.

It is not a hypervisor

A hypervisor is software that carves one physical server into what look like several. It fabricates a CPU, memory, disk and network card for each virtual machine. The OS on top believes it is installed on real hardware, which is why every VM needs its own OS installed.

VMware ESXi, Proxmox, Hyper-V and KVM are hypervisors. An AWS EC2 instance is one slice handed out by one. So is the VirtualBox you use to run a Linux on your laptop.

Docker does not carve up hardware. It isolates processes on a Linux kernel that is already running. Nothing to install, nothing to boot. They work differently, which does not make them incompatible: running Docker inside a VM is a common arrangement.

Virtual machine Container
What sits underneath A hypervisor The Docker engine
OS A guest OS per app Shares the host kernel
Size Gigabytes Tens to hundreds of megabytes
Startup Minutes Seconds

That is why containers are light. A container never boots an OS; it carves up the host kernel with Linux namespaces and cgroups.

Images and containers

An image is everything your app needs to run — code, runtime, system tools, libraries, settings — packed into one bundle. It is read-only, so running it a hundred times never changes what is inside.

A container is that image taken off the shelf and actually running. Stop it and remove it, and the image is still there. You can also start several containers from the one image.

Writing a Dockerfile

A Dockerfile records what goes into the image and how, in one file. Each line becomes one layer, stacked from the bottom up.

For a Java app it comes down to four decisions.

  1. Which runtime do I stand on → FROM
  2. Where does the jar go → WORKDIR + COPY
  3. How does it start → ENTRYPOINT
  4. What stays out of the image → .dockerignore

The instructions worth knowing

Instruction What it does
FROM The base image at the bottom. Almost always the first line
ARG A variable for build time only. It does not survive into the image
ENV An environment variable for the container. Also available during the build
WORKDIR The working directory for everything after it. Created if missing
COPY Copies a file from the host into the image
ADD COPY with extras — unpacks archives, fetches URLs. Unless you need that, use COPY
RUN Runs a command during the build (installing packages, compiling)
EXPOSE Documents the port this container uses. It does not actually open it
ENTRYPOINT The command that always runs when the container starts
CMD Default arguments for ENTRYPOINT. On its own, the default command
USER The account that runs everything after it. Without it, you are root

The simplest form

For a jar that is already built. The build happened outside, and Docker only packages it into an image.

The openjdk official image is no longer updated. For anything new, eclipse-temurin is the safe default. The -jre suffix means runtime only — no compiler, so it is smaller. Unless you are building inside the image, take -jre over -jdk.

Things that catch people out

  • The two forms of ENTRYPOINT. The exec form, ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"], is the default. No shell in between, so signals land directly on the Java process and the SIGTERM from docker stop reaches your app for a clean shutdown. The catch: variables like ${JAVA_OPTS} are not expanded. If you need them, wrap in sh -c — and write exec java ... so Java replaces the shell. Without exec, the shell stays as PID 1 and never passes the signal along. docker stop then waits ten seconds and kills it outright, leaving Exited (137). If stopping a container always takes ten seconds, suspect this. The app never gets to close connections or finish what it was doing.
  • Time zones. Base images are usually UTC. If log timestamps look hours off, check ENV TZ.
  • ARG and ENV are not the same thing. ARG comes in through docker build --build-arg and disappears when the build ends. ENV is baked into the image and visible inside the container — put a password there and anyone with the image reads it back out of docker inspect.
  • Put the lines that change most at the bottom. The layer cache is reused from the top down to the first difference. With COPY app.jar last, a new jar leaves every layer above it untouched.
  • Add a .dockerignore. Without one, the entire folder is shipped to the daemon as build context. Excluding just .git, build and .gradle cuts that down sharply.
  • Don’t run as root. For anything headed to production, create an account and drop to it with USER.

Build it and run it

1) Clear the way

To reuse the same name and tag, empty the slot first.

If an image refuses to go, a container is usually still holding it. Check docker ps -a and remove the container first.

2) Build

Go to the folder holding the Dockerfile.

  • -t myapp:1.0 — name and tag. Leave the tag off and you get latest.
  • The trailing . — the build context, meaning the current folder. Easy to forget.
  • --no-cache — throws the cache away and rebuilds from the bottom. You rarely need it and it only costs time. Reach for it when a file changed but kept the same path and name, and you suspect the cache is holding the old one.

3) Run and check

-f keeps streaming new output. Ctrl+C gets you out; the container keeps running.

4) Get inside

When the logs don’t settle it, go in and look. You can check that a config file landed, or that a mount actually attached.

  • -i keeps stdin open and -t attaches a terminal. A shell needs both. Drop either one and you get no prompt, or a prompt that ignores you.
  • exit when you’re done. The container keeps running.

You can also run a single command and come straight back out.

A few things worth knowing.

  • exec only works on a running container. One that died during startup is out of reach. Start a throwaway from the image instead — --rm cleans it up on exit.

    You need --entrypoint bash because otherwise the original ENTRYPOINT starts Java, which dies for the same reason it did the first time.

  • Permission denied? Go in as root. If the image drops to a non-root USER, you may not be able to read the log files.

  • Nothing you change in there survives. If editing a config inside the container fixed the problem, you have confirmed the cause, not fixed it. docker rm takes it with you. Carry the same change back to the mounted host folder or into the image.

Wrapping docker run in a script

Once the options run past a few lines, typing them by hand every time gets unreliable. Bury them in a script and run that instead.

Option Meaning
-d Run in the background
--name Container name. Without it Docker invents one
--restart unless-stopped Comes back up after a reboot
-p 8080:8080 hostPort:containerPort
-e KEY=VALUE Environment variable. Overrides ENV from the Dockerfile
-v hostPath:containerPath Volume mount
-v /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro Borrow the host’s clock. An alternative to -e TZ
-m 1g Memory ceiling. Only needed when several containers share a host

Remove a container and everything written inside it goes with it. Anything that has to survive — logs, config — belongs on a host folder mounted in. Then you can swap the container as often as you like. If your app also writes logs to file (a File Appender in logback or log4j2), mount that path out. Left inside, those logs only eat disk until the container takes them with it.

Moving an image as a .tar

For servers with no internet and no registry in reach, carry the image as a file.

  • docker save takes an image; docker export takes a container’s filesystem. To move an image, it is save. What comes out of export has lost its layers and metadata like ENTRYPOINT, so it will not simply run.
  • A tar is a bundle, not compression, so it is bulky. docker save myapp:1.0 | gzip > myapp.tar.gz if size matters.
  • load restores the image only. You still start the container with docker run.

The commands, in one place

To do this Run
Running containers docker ps
Including stopped ones docker ps -a
Stop a container docker stop {name}
Remove a container docker rm {name}
List images docker images
Remove an image docker image rm {imageID}
Build an image docker build -t {name}:{tag} .
Run a container docker run -d --name {name} -p 8080:8080 {image}:{tag}
Follow all logs docker logs -f {name}
Follow the last 100 lines docker logs -f -n 100 {name}
Get a shell inside docker exec -it {name} /bin/bash
Inspect the full config docker inspect {name}
Resource usage docker stats {name}
Image to file docker save -o {file}.tar {image}:{tag}
File to image docker load -i {file}.tar
Clean up what’s unused docker system prune

item.title: Connecting to a server and moving files
item.description: You can start connecting without installing anything. What you need after that is somewhere to save connections, and a way to move files.
item.content:encoded:
What a server is and which commands you run inside it are in the terminal post. This one covers what sits on either side of that: what you connect with, and how files get in and out.

A terminal and ssh are different levels

A terminal is the window where you type commands. ssh is a command you run in that window.

Choosing a terminal and connecting to a server are two separate things. Without that split, “install a terminal” and “connect to the server” collapse into one vague task.

Windows already ships ssh

Open PowerShell and type it.

The OpenSSH client has been included since Windows 10 1809. mac and Linux have had it in the default terminal all along. You can start without installing anything.

Starting here is the better order the first time. It keeps picking a client separate from finding out whether you can connect at all.

Why people still use a dedicated client

Four reasons.
Saved connections Once you have a few servers, typing IPs and usernames gets old
Tabs Several servers in one window
Key management Register private key paths and pick one
File transfer A terminal and SFTP in the same window

I use Termius. The screen for registering connections is well done, and dragging files to and from a server is easy. There are Windows, mac and Linux builds, and it is usable for free.

Other options worth knowing:

  • XShell with XFtp — widely used in Korea. The terminal and the file transfer are separate programs, and there is a free licence for home and school use
  • MobaXterm — opens an SFTP browser on the left alongside the SSH session
  • PuTTY — the old standard. Fewer features, but small and available everywhere
  • VS Code Remote-SSH — opens server files straight in the editor. The one to use if editing is the point

The fields you fill in

Menu names differ by client. The fields do not.

Field What goes in
Host, Address The server’s IP or domain
Port 22, or whatever it was changed to
Username The account to log in as
Password, Key The auth method. With a key, point it at the private key file
Label, Name The name shown in the list

Save it once and connecting is picking a row from a list. Past ten servers that alone pays for using a client.

Moving files

For pushing a jar up to a server or pulling a log down.

SFTP is file transfer riding on SSH. It generally works with no extra setup once SSH does, because there is no separate service to run on the server.

It is not FTP, despite the name. FTP has no encryption, and it needs its own service installed and running on the server.

scp — copy once and done

secure copy.

What follows the colon is the path on the server. Leave the colon out and it turns into a plain local copy, so it is worth a second look.

The . at the end means the current folder. It is the destination, so it cannot be left off.

sftp — connect and move around

The commands with an l in front act on your own machine — l for local. When you lose track of which side you are looking at, run pwd and lpwd one after the other.

Which one to use

Situation
A handful of files Dragging in a client’s SFTP view is quicker
Inside a script scp. One line, and the result comes back as an exit code
Large files, repeatedly rsync. Sends only what changed
Moving files within the server Connect and use cp or mv. No reason to route it through your machine

When permissions get in the way

If an uploaded file does not appear, or you cannot delete it, it is usually permissions.

scp and sftp write files as the account you connected with. Connect as dev and files only land where dev can write. If the folder is owned by root, you are blocked.

Two ways around it. Upload somewhere writable such as your home directory and move it with sudo mv on the server, or change the folder’s owner to dev up front.

Reading the permission string is covered in accounts and permissions in the terminal post.

The commands, in one place

To do this Run Short for
Connect ssh dev@host secure shell
On another port ssh -p 2222 dev@host port
With a specific key ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa dev@host identity
Upload a file scp file dev@host:/path/ secure copy
Download a file scp dev@host:/path/file . secure copy
A whole folder scp -r dir dev@host:/path/ recursive
Connect and transfer sftp dev@host ssh file transfer protocol
Send only what changed rsync -av dir/ dev@host:/path/ archive, verbose

item.title: The terminal, from what a server is to vi
item.description: Why programs die when an SSH session drops, where things live in the Linux directory tree, and vi's three modes — in that order.
item.content:encoded:
SSH into a server and you get one line:

I knew ls and cd and still got stuck right here. I did not know where I was, or what the inside of this server looked like. Learning more commands was not going to fix that kind of stuck.

So this starts before the command list. What a server is, where files go, and then the commands.

Abbreviations are spelled out as they come up. Knowing rm is remove is one less thing to memorise.

What a server is

A computer with no screen and no keyboard. That is genuinely the only difference from the PC on your desk. It is powered on, an OS is running, programs are up — there is just no monitor attached.

Which means you need another way in.

Connecting over SSH

ssh is secure shell, an encrypted shell. What the command does is start a shell on that other machine and pipe its input and output to your screen. Type ls and you get that machine’s files.

There are two ways to prove who you are:

  • Password — you type the account’s password
  • Key — you use a key pair made in advance. The public key is registered on the server and the private key stays on the machine you connect from

Which program you connect with, and how to move files, are covered separately.

Closing the session kills the programs

Connecting over SSH creates a session. Programs you start there hang off that session. Close the window, shut the laptop, lose the network, and the session dies — and so do the programs hanging off it.

Closing the window while watching logs costs nothing; tail dies but the log file is untouched. This is the case that costs something:

So anything meant to keep running does not hang off a session. In the Docker post I described the -d in docker run -d as “run it in the background”. More precisely it is detached — never attached to a session in the first place. That is why a container keeps running after you close the SSH window.

Where you are, and paths

Windows Explorer always shows the path at the top, so you never have to ask where you are. A terminal has no such display, which is why asking is a command of its own.

pwd is print working directory.

Reading the prompt

Most of the time you do not need pwd. It is already written in front of the cursor.

A ~ in the position field means your home directory. Typing /home/dev every time gets old, so ~ stands in for it.

Absolute and relative paths

Written as Meaning
/opt/myapp/log An absolute path, written from the top /. Points at the same place wherever you run it
log or ./log A relative path, from where you are. . is the current folder
../config .. is one level up. Go up, then into config
~/notes notes under your home

Scripts are safer with absolute paths, since they have to point at the same place no matter where they are run from.

The directory tree

Linux folder names are fixed by convention, so the same things sit in the same places from server to server.

Path What is in it
/home/dev The dev account’s home. You land here when you log in
/etc System configuration files
/var/log Logs. /var is variable — things whose contents keep changing
/opt optional. Software installed separately. A common home for apps you built yourself
/usr Software the distribution installed. /usr/bin holds the commands
/tmp Temporary files. Gone after a reboot, so nothing important goes here

/ is the top of the tree; /root is the root account’s home directory. Similar names, different places.

pwd, ls, cd

Command Short for
ls list
cd change directory

ls is usually run with options, and the options are abbreviations too.

cd has a few shortcuts worth knowing.

Tab and the arrow keys

Two keys that never make it into a command list but get used constantly.

Tab completes a path from a partial one. Press it twice when several things match and you get the list.

Up arrow brings back the last command you ran. Keep pressing to walk further back. It is what you reach for when a long command needs one small change.

Working with files

Command Short for What it does
mkdir make directory Creates a folder
touch touch Its actual job is updating a file’s timestamp. Point it at a file that does not exist and an empty one appears, which is the side effect people use it for
cp copy Copy
mv move Move
rm remove Delete

One mv does both renaming and moving. What identifies a file is its path plus its name — change the name and it is a rename, change the path and it is a move. Same operation, so one command.

rm does not ask

No recycle bin, no “are you sure”. It is done the moment you press enter.

Here is the usual shape of an accident with -rf:

Misspell the variable, or let a script run before it is set, and $DIR expands to nothing — leaving rm -rf /. Which is why scripts turn undefined variables into errors with set -u and check the path is not empty before deleting.

Looking at file contents

Command When
cat A short file, all of it
head Just the start
tail Just the end
less A long file, one screen at a time

cat is catenate — it prints several files joined together. Give it one file and you get that one, which is how it came to be used for reading.

cat on a log file sends tens of thousands of lines past the screen. Long files go to less or tail. Inside less the arrow keys scroll, /text searches, and q quits.

vi

For editing a file on a server. vi is short for visual.

vi has three modes. The same key does different things in each, so you need to know which one you are in.

It opens in command mode, where every key is a command and typing inserts nothing. Type a sentence in this state and each character runs as a command.

Starting to type

Key Short for What it does
i insert Start typing at the cursor
a append Start typing after the cursor
o open line Open a blank line below and start typing
Esc Stop typing, back to command mode

Saving and quitting

Press : and a colon appears on the bottom line, where you type the command.

Short for
:w write Save
:q quit Quit
:wq write + quit Save and quit. The one you use most
:q! forced quit Leave without saving. The way out when you have broken something

Working by lines (in command mode)

Key Short for What it does
dd delete Cut the line the cursor is on. It goes to the clipboard
yy yank Copy the line the cursor is on
p put Paste below the cursor
P Capital pastes above
u undo Undo the last thing
Ctrl+r redo Redo what you undid

dd is d twice because d is the delete command and a range follows it. d + d is “one line”, d + 3d is “three lines”. yy works the same way.

Not sure which mode you are in? Press Esc twice. You end up in command mode either way.

nano

Run something like crontab -e on an Ubuntu or Debian server and nano opens instead of vi. It is the default editor on that side.

nano has no modes. It opens ready to type, with the shortcuts always shown along the bottom. There is almost nothing to learn.

There is exactly one trap. In ^X Exit along the bottom, ^ means Ctrl. That is where people go looking for a ^ key.
Ctrl+O Save (write Out)
Ctrl+X Quit (eXit)
Ctrl+K Cut a line
Ctrl+U Paste
Ctrl+W Search (Where is)

The editor a server definitely has is vi. It is in the POSIX standard, so it survives even a minimal install, which is why the weight belongs on vi. Plenty of servers open nano first though, and knowing that ^ is Ctrl is enough to not be stuck there.

Reading logs and finding files

These two are most of what you do once you are on a server.

Following a log live

  • -f — follow. Stays at the end of the file and shows new lines as they arrive
  • -n 100 — number. Starts from the last 100 lines, then follows
  • Ctrl+C to get out

Docker container logs take the same options. docker logs -f -n 100 looking identical is not a coincidence.

One overlap to watch: the f in tail -f is follow, but the f in rm -f is force. Same letter, different meaning per command.

Searching inside files

grep is globally search a regular expression and print.

  • -r — recursive, into subfolders
  • -n — number, which line it was on
  • -i — ignore case
  • --include="*.log" — only certain extensions

Piping is common too.

| hands the output of the left command to the right one as input. That line means “of the last 1000 lines, only the ones containing ERROR”.

Accounts and permissions

Linux has one account that can do anything: root. Nothing stops it from deleting system files.

So you do not work as root. You log in as a normal account and borrow the privilege when you need it, which limits how far a mistake spreads. The last character of the prompt tells you which side you are on.

Touching a file you do not have permission for stops here:

That is when sudo runs that one line as root. substitute user do — run as another account, defaulting to root.

Stay logged in as root and every command is unlimited; nothing catches a mistyped rm -rf. With sudo, that one line runs as root and everything else stays on the normal account.

Three groups of permissions per file

The first ten characters of ls -l are the permissions.

They come in groups of three.

Letter Short for On a file On a directory
r read Can read the contents Can list what is inside
w write Can change the contents Can create and delete files inside
x execute Can run it Can enter the folder

Read the example above and app.yml can only be changed by its owner dev, with everyone else limited to reading. config is owned by root, so the dev account can go in and look but cannot create files there.

There is a numeric form too: r is 4, w is 2, x is 1, added up per group.

Number Letters Meaning
755 rwxr-xr-x Owner does everything, everyone else reads and runs. Common on executables and folders
644 rw-r--r-- Owner writes, everyone else reads. The usual default for a plain file
600 rw------- Only the owner reads and writes. For files nobody else should see

chmod

change mode.

The first line is the earlier point in practice: a file does not run because of its extension, it runs because the execute permission is there. With it, ./docker_run.sh works; without it you hand the file to bash as bash docker_run.sh.

The second line is an SSH private key. If its permissions are open, ssh refuses to use the key.

chown and Docker volumes

change owner.

When an app running as root inside a container writes logs into a mounted host folder, those files come out owned by root on the host too.

You can handle each case with sudo, but the real fix is not running the container as root. Drop to an account with USER in the image and the files are owned by that account from the start. This is where “don’t run as root” from the Docker post leads.

The commands, in one place

To do this Run Short for
Where am I pwd print working directory
List ls -lah list / long, all, human
Move cd path change directory
One level up cd ..
Back to the last one cd -
Make a folder mkdir -p path make directory / parents
Make an empty file touch name
Copy cp -r src dest copy / recursive
Move or rename mv src dest move
Delete rm -rf path remove / recursive, force
Read a file cat name catenate
Start of a file head -n 20 name
End of a file tail -n 100 name
Follow a log tail -f -n 100 name follow
Page through less name
Edit vi name visual
Search grep -rn "text" path regular expression + print
Run as admin sudo command substitute user do
See permissions ls -l name long
Add execute permission chmod +x name change mode
Change owner sudo chown dev:dev name change owner

item.title: How this blog is put together
item.description: Astro emits the static HTML, the Starlight docs theme sits on top, and a blog plugin turns it into a blog. Search, table of contents, dark mode and i18n come with the theme.
item.content:encoded:
This blog runs in Korean and English. Here’s what it’s made of.

The pieces

What it does
Astro Emits static HTML at build time. Almost no JavaScript reaches the browser.
Starlight Astro’s official docs theme — search, table of contents, dark mode and i18n included.
starlight-blog Adds a blog on top of the docs theme: post lists, tags, RSS.
GitHub Pages Push to main and Actions builds and publishes it.

Two requirements: run in Korean and English, and be findable in search.

Building the routing and the language switcher by hand would have been more work than taking something that already does it. As for search, here’s what ends up in the build output.

hreflang tells search engines the Korean and English pages are the same post in two languages; without it they can be read as duplicate content. A sitemap is generated alongside.

Static HTML does the rest. This post’s body is readable without running a single line of JavaScript — a crawler receives a finished document, not an empty <div>.

That only means the groundwork is in place. Whether anything ranks is a separate question, answered after there are posts and the site is registered with search engines.

Korean and English

Korean sits at the root, English under /en/.

Two files that share a name are treated as translations of each other, so the language button takes you to the same post in the other language.

When a translation doesn’t exist yet, Starlight shows the default-language content instead. There’s no setting to turn that off, so those pages carry a noindex — otherwise search engines would index Korean text as an English page. Adding a real translation clears it automatically.

Filing posts

Posts are filed with tags.

The sidebar groups them under a parent category according to the tree in src/categories.ts. Tags that aren’t in the tree collect under Other, which is the cue to give them a place.

What a post looks like

description and excerpt do different jobs: the first is for search engines and link previews, the second is what a person reads in the list. Leave excerpt out and the whole post body lands in the list.

Setting draft: true keeps a post visible locally and out of the build, so an unfinished draft can be committed without going public.

Publishing

Push to main. The build output is never committed.

The workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/deploy.yml. Astro ships an official action, so there isn’t much to write.

Leave out the permissions and the deploy step refuses to run.

What trips people up

  • A 404 — check whether Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source is still on Deploy from a branch. That’s the default, and until it’s switched the workflow can run all it likes without anything going live.
  • Broken CSS — the site value in astro.config.mjs doesn’t match the real address. If the repository isn’t named <username>.github.io, you also need base: '/repository-name/'.
  • A post that doesn’t show up — malformed frontmatter fails the build. The content schema catches it, and the Actions log names the file and the field.
